concept_name: Solids of Revolution: Spinning a Flat Region and Finding Its Volume
section: Volumes of solids of revolution (the disc and ring methods). NCERT Class 12 Chapter 8 'Application of Integrals' is the nearest Indian index entry and covers AREA under simple curves only -- volumes of revolution are NOT in the current CBSE Class-12 or JEE Main scope. This concept is authored for AP Calculus AB/BC, A-level Pure, IB DP AA HL and ISC, where the topic IS examined. See curriculum_tags: every cell is a CLAIM (Rule 38g).
source_book: Chapter-index scope reference only (NCERT Class 12 Mathematics Ch. 8; AP Calculus AB/BC and A-level Pure topic lists for the volumes-of-revolution scope). Teaching sequence, examples and every phrasing authored first-hand -- no prose, figure or worked example is imported from any source.

real_world_anchor.primary: A drinking glass: its outside surface is one curve turned about the glass's own axis, which is exactly what this concept does. The same object in every country and every classroom, so it carries no country-specific culture (Rule 35a) and it is not lab apparatus, which gives it the widest possible syllabus overlap (Rule 38f).
real_world_anchor.secondary: The anchor is SPOKEN and never DRAWN. The sim's curve is y = √x, not a glass profile, so no axis is labelled 'height' or 'width' and no tumbler is modelled.

a.name: the curve's height coefficient in y = a√x (STATE_9 only)

b.name: the far end of the interval -- the upper limit of integration and the far end of the solid

n.name: number of discs in the stack (STATE_9 only; the guided states drive n from their own ramps)

r.name: the sphere's radius on STATE_5. Quantised to the slider step 0.01 on BOTH drive paths, which makes the reachable set exactly 101 values -- a finite set the gate enumerates rather than samples

x_cut.name: where STATE_3's single disc cuts the solid

formulas.region_area: A = integral of f(x) dx over [0, b]; for f = sqrt(x) on [0, 4] this is 16/3 = 5.3333
formulas.slice_face_area: pi * f(x)^2; at x = 1 this is pi = 3.1416, at x = 4 it is 4pi = 12.5664
formulas.disc_sum: V_n = pi * sum over i of f(x_i)^2 * dx, LEFT rule; for f = sqrt(x) on [0, 4] this is 8pi(n-1)/n exactly, because f squared is linear
formulas.exact_volume_about_x: V = pi * integral of f(x)^2 dx = 8pi = 25.1327 on [0, 4]
formulas.gap: V - V_n = 8pi/n exactly -- ONE term, which is why this profile was chosen
formulas.sphere: spinning y = sqrt(r^2 - x^2) on [-r, r] gives V = 4/3 pi r^3; its LEFT disc sum is 4/3 pi r^3 (1 - 1/n^2)
formulas.ring: V = pi * integral of (R^2 - r^2) dx; outer sqrt(x), inner x/2 on [0, 4] gives 8pi/3 = 8.3776
formulas.ring_wrong_M2: pi * integral of (R - r)^2 dx = 0.5333pi = 1.6755 -- the misconception, built on purpose so the wrong number is reproducible rather than hand-typed
formulas.limits: V(b) = pi * integral of x dx over [0, b] = pi b^2 / 2; b = 2 gives 6.2832, b = 4 gives 25.1327

constraints: DOMAIN FIRST. y = a*sqrt(x) is defined only for x >= 0, and every state that draws it authors a domain starting at 0 -- no caption generalises past the interval actually drawn.

The semicircle y = sqrt(r^2 - x^2) is defined ONLY on [-r, r]. STATE_5 sweeps r, and the drawn domain is DERIVED from the profile's own support rather than authored beside it, so the two are incapable of disagreeing. Authoring a fixed [-2, 2] there would draw a flat line where no curve exists and print a non-finite exact volume.

The disc rule is LEFT in every state, and midpoint is never used or mentioned. On this profile f squared is LINEAR, so the MIDPOINT rule is exact (8pi at every n) and a state teaching convergence would be showing a gap that does not exist.

STATE_5 needs n = 20000, not 1000: at n = 1000 the disc total and 4/3 pi r cubed disagree in the fourth decimal at 13 of the 101 reachable radii. At 20000 the analytic gap is at most 8.378e-8, four orders below the 1e-4 display quantum, and 0 of 101 disagree.
STATE_6 needs n >= 1000 for its two totals to print the values the lesson names: at n = 500 the ring total renders 8.3775, not 8.3776.
Volumes and areas are unitless -- they are measured in the plane's own units, and no physical unit is asserted anywhere in this concept.

aha_moment.statement: The disc total equals four thirds pi r cubed at every radius.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: The ball grows as r sweeps 1.00 to 2.00 and the two HUD lines print the same four decimals at all 101 radii the slider can reach -- 33.5103 against 33.5103 at r = 2.00, 14.1372 against 14.1372 at r = 1.50.

misconception_watch.belief: Spinning a region of area A gives a volume of π times A, so the volume here is π × 5.3333 = 16.7552.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The HUD carries π × area = 16.7552 beside the true face area 3.1416 at x = 1. The travelling disc's radius is marked as the curve HEIGHT, so what spins is a radius, never an area.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: The curve's height is the radius, and a circle's area needs that radius squared.

tts_sentences.text_en: One common expectation is that spinning an area gives pi times that area.
Cut the solid across at one x instead. The face is a circle.
Its radius is the curve height, so the face area is pi r squared.

misconception_watch.belief: For a region between two curves you subtract the radii and spin the difference: π ∫ (R − r)² dx, giving 1.6755.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The sim BUILDS that solid first and reads 1.6755, then dissolves it and builds the ring stack, which reads 8.3776 -- five times bigger. The removed circle is not a shorter radius, it is a missing middle.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Take away the inner circle's area, not the inner radius.

tts_sentences.text_en: A drinking glass is hollow, so the solid part is the material between two curves.
One wrong method subtracts the radii first and spins the difference. It reads 1.6755.
Each slice is really a ring, or washer: take away the inner circle's area, not the inner radius.

assessment.mastery_definition: A student has mastered this concept when they can say what solid a given region sweeps out about a given line, write the slice area as pi times a radius SQUARED, recognise that a finite disc total approaches but never reaches the exact volume, subtract inner AREA rather than inner radius for a ring, and read the two limits of an integral as the two ends of the solid.

questions.stem: The flat region under y = √x on [0, 4] is turned one full turn about the x-axis. What does it sweep out?

options.A: A solid that gets wider along the axis
options.B: A flat disc -- the region simply rotated inside its own plane
options.C: A hollow tube with nothing inside it
options.D: A cube whose side is the region's width

distractor_misconceptions.B: Reads the turn as a rotation WITHIN the plane, so the region never leaves two dimensions and no volume is swept.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Assumes every solid of revolution is hollow, when a hole appears only if a second curve bounds the region away from the axis.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Treats the sweep as an extrusion in a straight line rather than a turn about an axis.

questions.tested_idea: turning a flat region about a line sweeps out a solid
questions.parallel_form_stem: The region under y = √x on [0, 9] is turned one full turn about the x-axis. What shape results?

questions.stem: Cut that solid across the axis at x = 4. The cut face is a circle. Its area is:

distractor_misconceptions.B: Uses 2πr instead of πr² -- the circumference formula where the area one is needed.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Stops at the radius itself, √4 = 2, without turning it into an area at all.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Reports the flat region's area 16/3, which is a property of the region, not of one circular slice.

questions.tested_idea: the slice face area is pi times the radius SQUARED
questions.parallel_form_stem: Cut the same solid at x = 1. What is the area of the circular face there?

questions.stem: Four left-hand discs give 18.85 and the exact volume is 25.13. One hundred discs give:

options.D: 18.85 -- the disc count does not change the total

distractor_misconceptions.B: Treats 'approaches' as 'reaches', so a finite sum is taken to land on the limit rather than close in on it.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Assumes the left-hand sum overshoots. On an increasing radius every left disc is too small, so the total stays below.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Reads the disc count as a drawing choice rather than as what the total is computed from.

questions.tested_idea: a finite disc total approaches the exact volume from below and never reaches it
questions.parallel_form_stem: Twenty left-hand discs give 23.88 against an exact 25.13. Do one thousand discs give more, less, or exactly 25.13?

questions.stem: Turn the semicircle y = √(4 − x²) on [−2, 2] about the x-axis. The volume is:

distractor_misconceptions.B: Uses 4πr², the surface area of a sphere, where the volume formula is needed.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Multiplies the flat semicircle's area by π -- the same missing-square error as spinning an area.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Carries over the earlier answer 8π from a different curve, as though every solid of revolution shared one volume.

questions.tested_idea: a semicircle turned about its diameter gives a ball of volume four thirds pi r cubed
questions.parallel_form_stem: Turn y = √(9 − x²) on [−3, 3] about the x-axis. What volume results?

questions.stem: The region between y = √x and y = x/2 on [0, 4] is turned about the x-axis. The volume is:

distractor_misconceptions.B: Subtracts the RADII and spins the difference, π∫(R − r)² dx, instead of subtracting the two circle AREAS.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Ignores the inner curve entirely and reports the solid volume as though the region reached the axis.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Substitutes the sphere answer from the previous state, which belongs to a different region and a different curve.

questions.tested_idea: for a region between two curves each slice is a ring and the inner AREA is subtracted
questions.parallel_form_stem: The region between y = √x and y = x/2 on [0, 4] is turned about the x-axis. Is each slice a disc or a ring, and what is subtracted?

questions.stem: The same region under y = √x on [0, 4], turned about the y-axis instead, gives:

options.D: It cannot be turned about the y-axis

distractor_misconceptions.B: Treats the volume as a property of the region alone, so the choice of axis is assumed not to matter.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Confuses the other-axis solid with the ring solid, since both are built from rings.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Assumes a region can only be turned about the axis it was drawn against.

questions.tested_idea: the axis of revolution is part of the question and changes the solid and its volume
questions.parallel_form_stem: Turning the region under y = √x on [0, 4] about the y-axis instead of the x-axis gives a larger, smaller, or identical volume?

questions.stem: In V = π ∫₀ᵇ (√x)² dx, changing b from 4 to 2 changes the volume from 25.13 to:

distractor_misconceptions.B: Halves the volume with b, when the volume goes as b squared -- halving b quarters it.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Reads the limits as labels on the picture rather than as the two ends the volume is computed between.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Divides by four but starts from π rather than from πb²/2.

questions.tested_idea: the limits of the integral are the two ends of the solid, and the volume goes as b squared
questions.parallel_form_stem: In V = π ∫₀ᵇ (√x)² dx, what happens to the volume when b is changed from 4 to 3?
